reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its observable purpose is teaching viewers how to create and manage a YouTube channel, including channel setup and YouTube Studio analytics. Although the description advertises the creator's courses through an external form, the available video evidence characterizes this as ordinary educational commerce without a deceptive promise, required financial participation, or particular outcome. The unclear upload statement appears in copyright and monetization guidance that also tells viewers not to upload copyrighted videos, so it does not establish a scam mechanism.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the income framing and the action requested together. The title offers a course on earning money from YouTube, while the description tells viewers to buy the creator's courses through an external form. The speaker also says viewers who follow the advice can gain subscribers and eventually withdraw payment. That makes the paid-course invitation more consequential than an incidental link: it is placed beside a path from learning the method to receiving money. The evidence does not show that buying is required, but the solicitation benefits from that income expectation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The channel-creation and upload demonstrations establish that the video contains instruction; they do not settle what the income framing does for the course solicitation. The description puts the purchase link before its outline of the lessons. Nor does the absence of a stated guarantee make the invitation irrelevant: the speaker connects applying his advice to gaining subscribers, then discusses withdrawing money. The defense is right that purchase is not shown as a prerequisite, but that limits the claim; it does not erase the promotional linkage.

opening.argument: Judge, the concern is the combination of signals. An external purchase form appears in the description of a money-making course. In the lesson, the speaker presents his own thumbnail as having gone viral and urges viewers to make clickable thumbnails to gain subscribers early. He also gives an unclear three-second copyright instruction immediately before warning that longer uploads can prevent monetization. Those details could make the route to income seem easier or more controllable than the evidence establishes. The transcript does not prove a working shortcut, but its ambiguity matters when paired with the paid invitation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense reads the upload passage in its surrounding copyright warning, which is important context. But that context does not resolve the speaker's precise three-second claim: he still pairs a duration with a monetization consequence. Likewise, genuine Studio instruction does not validate the unusually strong thumbnail anecdote or explain what buying through the external form provides. These points do not prove deception individually; together, they warrant scrutiny of how confidently the video presents a path toward earnings.
